questions.prompt: How many of the 3 user rows does the query below return?

choices.rationale: No user is literally named "' OR '1'='1", so a single matching row would only happen if the input were treated as data.
Zero rows is what a safe parameterized query returns; here the injected OR clause matches everything.

choices.text: The query raises a syntax error
choices.rationale: The payload is crafted to stay syntactically valid: the quotes balance out into a complete WHERE clause.

questions.code:
users table: alice, bob, carol

user_input = "' OR '1'='1"
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + user_input + "'"

query.explanation: Because the input is pasted straight into the SQL text, its quote closes the name literal and adds `OR '1'='1'`, a condition that is always true. The WHERE clause therefore matches every row, so all 3 users are returned instead of none.
query.syntax: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1'
query.title: Classic tautology injection

questions.prompt: Does the parameterized query below return zero rows for that payload?
questions.code:
users table: alice, bob, carol

con.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", ("' OR '1'='1",))

query.explanation: With a bound parameter the driver sends the payload as a single string value, so the database looks for a user literally named "' OR '1'='1". No such row exists, so the result set is empty.
query.title: Parameters treat input as data

questions.rationale: False would mean the payload still altered the query structure, but a bound parameter is never parsed as SQL, so it only matches a user whose name is that exact string.

questions.prompt: Which placeholder does Python's sqlite3 module use for positional parameters?

Dollar-numbered placeholders belong to PostgreSQL's wire protocol and node-postgres, not Python's sqlite3.
Numeric-colon placeholders come from paramstyle 'numeric' (e.g. some Oracle drivers); sqlite3 reports 'qmark'.

query.explanation: sqlite3 reports paramstyle 'qmark', meaning positional parameters are written as `?`. Knowing the right placeholder matters because developers often fall back to string formatting when they guess the wrong style.
query.title: Placeholder styles

All three rows would need an always-true condition; here the name filter on 'alice' still applies.
The statement is valid SQL: the trailing text is simply a comment, so parsing succeeds.

-- users table has 3 rows: alice, bob, carol
SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE name = 'alice' --' AND password = 'nope';

query.explanation: The attacker's input ends with `--`, which starts a SQL line comment. Everything after it, including the password check, is ignored, so the query matches the single row for alice without verifying the password.

allow.test(input)

Number.isInteger(Number(input))

-- users table has 3 rows: alice, bob, carol
SELECT name FROM users UNION SELECT 'attacker'

query.explanation: A UNION appends the rows of a second SELECT to the first result set, so three real users plus one attacker-supplied row give 4 rows. This is how attackers graft extra data onto a legitimate query's output.
query.syntax: SELECT col FROM t UNION SELECT 'value'
query.title: UNION-based injection

questions.rationale: False would mean the extra SELECT contributes nothing, but its distinct value 'attacker' is added to the three distinct user names, making 4 rows.

questions.prompt: Can a table name be passed as a `?` parameter to sqlite3's execute()?
questions.code: con.execute("SELECT * FROM ?", ("users",))

query.explanation: Placeholders bind values, not identifiers, so `FROM ?` is a syntax error. Table and column names must be chosen from a fixed allow-list in your code rather than taken from user input.
query.title: Parameters cannot replace identifiers

questions.rationale: True would mean the driver substitutes the name into the FROM clause, but placeholders only carry data values, so the statement fails to parse.

questions.prompt: The users table holds ('bob', active = false) and ('amy', active = true). The injected comment cuts off the active filter. Does the query below print a count of 1?

SELECT count(*) FROM users
WHERE name = 'bob' --' AND active = false

query.explanation: The input `bob' --` closed the name literal and started a SQL line comment, so `AND active = false` is never evaluated. The query becomes just `WHERE name = 'bob'`, which matches the single bob row even though that row has active = false.
query.title: Comment payloads discard the rest of a query line

questions.rationale: The claim is true: `--` comments out the remainder of the line, so the active = false filter is dropped and the bob row still matches `name = 'bob'`, giving a count of 1 instead of 0.

cmd = "ping -c 1 " + host

A pipe starts another command and feeds it the previous command's output.

subprocess.run(args, shell=False)

A pipe chains a second command and passes output to it.

questions.rationale: 169.254.0.0/16 is the IPv4 link-local block, and the metadata IP 169.254.169.254 falls inside it, so is_link_local is True, not False.

print(urlparse("http://expected.example.com@169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/").hostname)

questions.prompt: Do the two salted hashes of the same password below match?
questions.code:
import hashlib

pw = "hunter2"
a = hashlib.sha256(b"salt1" + pw.encode()).hexdigest()
b = hashlib.sha256(b"salt2" + pw.encode()).hexdigest()
print(a == b)

query.explanation: The salt is hashed together with the password, so the same password hashed with salt1 and salt2 produces two different digests. That is the whole point of salting: identical passwords no longer share a stored hash, which defeats precomputed rainbow tables and makes it impossible to spot users who share a password.
query.title: Per-user salts change the digest

questions.rationale: They cannot match: the salt bytes are part of the hashed input, so changing the salt changes the digest even for an identical password.

questions.prompt: Does the Basic auth header below decode to the password s3cret?

import base64

header = "Basic dXNlcjpzM2NyZXQ="

questions.rationale: Base64 is reversible encoding rather than encryption, so the header decodes straight back to user:s3cret and the password is s3cret.

key = b"k1"
signed = json.dumps({"user": "bob", "admin": False})

Parameterized queries are still preferred; quote_literal is for cases where SQL text must be built dynamically.

questions.prompt: What does the abspath call below print?

query.explanation: os.path.abspath normalizes the path lexically: starting at /var/www/uploads, the three ../ segments climb past uploads, www, and var to the root, leaving /etc/passwd. This is why joining user input into a path and then normalizing can silently escape the intended upload directory — the escape must be detected after normalization, not before.
